title: Allahu akbar, thirty-four
hookLine: the Prophet ﷺ taught this set to his daughter Fatimah instead of a servant (Bukhari)
last: SA'ATAN WA SA'ATAN — AN HOUR, AND AN HOUR.

cards: Think of the most tired you've ever been from work with your hands. Moving house. A double shift.
A newborn at three in the morning. Now picture a young woman in Medina, her hands blistered from turning a stone hand mill every day, grinding grain for bread, and from hauling water.
She's the Prophet's ﷺ youngest daughter, Fatimah. She hears that some servants have come to Medina, and she goes to her father to ask for one. Just one.
Today: what he gave her instead.

teach.b: The story is in Bukhari and Muslim, told by her husband Ali. Fatimah went to the Prophet's house, but he wasn't there, so she told his wife Aisha why she'd come.
That night, after Fatimah and Ali had gone to bed, the Prophet came to their house. They started to get up.
Stay where you are, he said, and sat down between them. Ali remembered the coolness of his feet.

teach.h: SOMETHING BETTER THAN WHAT YOU ASKED.
teach.b: Then: shall I tell you something better than what you asked for? When you go to bed, say Allahu akbar thirty-four times, subhanallah thirty-three times, and alhamdulillah thirty-three times.
That is better for you than a servant. A hundred in all. It's a strange answer, if you're tired.
She asked for help with the work, and he gave her words. But look at the words.

teach.h: BETTER FOR YOU THAN A SERVANT.
teach.b: Greater than the mill, the tiredness, whatever the day took out of you. And he didn't send it with a messenger. He came himself, at night, and sat on the edge of their bed to teach them.

Ali said he never stopped saying it, not one night, even in the middle of a war. So the set that closes many Muslims' prayers, thirty-three, thirty-three, thirty-three or thirty-four, has a family story inside it.
A tired daughter. A father at the bedside. A gift that doesn't wear out, costs nothing, and is there when the servant isn't.

how: Many Muslims say Allahu akbar thirty-four times, with subhanallah and alhamdulillah thirty-three times each, when going to bed, following the set taught to Fatimah, and a similar hundred after the daily prayers.

o: a greeting meaning God be with you
God is greater than anything else
a blessing said after someone sneezes

games.q: who did what in the story — tap the pairs.
p: sat down between them at night

s: the Prophet ﷺ gave Fatimah the servant she asked for
he taught her the hundred at bedtime and said it was better for her than a servant.
the Prophet came to their house himself, at night
they'd gone to bed; he told them to stay and sat down between them.
in this set, Allahu akbar is said thirty-four times
thirty-four takbir, thirty-three tasbih, thirty-three tahmid: a hundred.

games.q: you're Fatimah. your hands are blistered from the mill, and you've asked your father for a servant. he comes at night. what does he give you?
o: words to say at bedtime, better than a servant
games.why: he taught Allahu akbar thirty-four times, subhanallah and alhamdulillah thirty-three each: better for you than a servant (Bukhari, Muslim).

practice: Whether you've just prayed or simply have two minutes, rest your right hand, palm up.

Count the full hundred on your finger joints, twice around the hand and a little more for each: thirty-three of subhanallah, glory, thirty-three of alhamdulillah, praise, thirty-four of Allahu akbar, greater.
If you don't pray, count the numbers, and on the last set, hold the thing that tired you most this week next to the words.

wordCard.voice: Allahu akbar. God is greater, thirty-four times, the last of the three, the gift given to Fatimah instead of a servant. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: God is greater, the thirty-four of the bedtime set.

carryVoice: Your line: better than a servant. Many still say Fatimah's hundred at bedtime. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 3113, 3705, 5361 (Fatimah asks for a servant; the hundred at bedtime)
Sahih Muslim 2727 (the same, with Ali's remark that he never left it)
